chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
title: After-school programs, volunteers and teachers
summary: She describes the programs for children, volunteer parents, and teachers' reactions.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: service these children after school for a nominal fee, 50¢ or something like that. But they had to go at a certain time and they had to make an appointment so I was in charge of seeing the kids and getting their parents to come in and signing the release, their permission for having them treated and then seeing that the kids got to the dentist on time, setting up the appointments. So I found working with the Parents Association very interesting. And so we went to work, all out to get more members in the Association so we'd have more people involved because there was a lot of things to be done. The cake sales, the book sales, they seemed fringed benefits, but we found that when the kids see their parents in the school participating, it makes them do a little better. You know, they feel their parents are interested. We had one little boy who insisted upon paying his mother's dues which was a dollar a year, and he would make every Parents Association Meeting, you know, because the Parents Association meets once a month. And every month he would come up wanting to pay his mother's dues. I said, it's not like that. I said, we want your mother here. So sure enough one evening she came

and he was busy pointing his mother out, you know, to the members of the Parents Association. So we got the membership up to about 200. And we really saw a great improvement in the kids. The kids would come down to the cake sale and saw their parents there. 'That's my mother,' you know. And the book fairs. And at the same time there are alot of workshops that we offer to parents to let them know just exactly what goes on in the schools. There are times when decisions have to be made. You know, what courses are the kids going to take. Sometimes the kids say, I want to be so and so, so and so, and they just haven't studied those particular subjects. They are not good enough in those subjects to even consider the course that they want to take. So this is where the parent and teacher can get together and say, this is what he needs. And then of course, at home when he comes up and says, I want to be a doctor, mom can say, well look, what are you going to do about your Science, or what are you going to do about this? And we get the kid in the middle. We don't put him in the middle, he puts us in the middle. So anyway, it was very interesting and I really enjoyed it. We wound up, a crew of us, we

started as all volunteers of course, and after they saw the parents, and at that time the schools were overcrowded and there was a shortage of teachers and they needed allot of help, especially for the things like monitoring the cafeteria and monitoring the hallways and things. So, as a result of the volunteer effort on the part of these parents they inaugurated the school aid program. The former volunteers could get paid, getting a $1.65 an hour working every day but a couple of hours a day just to take care of maybe the lunch passes or monitoring the cafeteria. And then, of course, there came about what they called The Career Opportunity Program where parents, or these interested people who came and worked as school aids to pursue a course and you become an Educational Assistant which means that they could go into the classroom and work with a teacher. At first there was a certain amount of resistance on the part of the teachers because of a lot of reasons they felt this would be just another problem. They didn't call them Educational Assistants, they called them Family Workers. This meant that if the kid was truant or if there was a problem the Family Worker was supposed to contact the
